subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: confessing late after first lying [Revision]
passage: After dinner Rafael said, "Mama, my homework is done," and went to watch cartoons. But the words followed him around the room like a stray dog. The cartoons stopped being funny. At half past eight he stood at the door of Lindiwe's bedroom with his reading book behind his back. "Mama, I lied. I have not done the reading or the spelling." His mother put down her knitting. "Thank you for telling me. I am not happy about the lie, but I am glad you came. Now get your book. Twenty minutes tonight, and the rest tomorrow." Rafael felt lighter, even holding the book.

qa.q: What did Rafael say he had not done?
qa.a: He said he had not done the reading or the spelling.

qa.q: How did Rafael feel after saying his homework was done?
qa.a: Guilty, because the words followed him around the room and spoiled the cartoons.

qa.q: What could Rafael do in future to avoid the same trap?
qa.a: Say honestly how much is left and ask for time, because telling the truth first avoids the guilt.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel about the confession?
qa.a: Displeased about the lie but glad that he came, since she thanked him and still asked him to finish the work.

grounding: A boy lies about homework, feels bad all evening, confesses before bed, and his mother thanks him but still expects the work.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: confessing late after first lying [Revision]
passage: Rafiq's mother was the matron of the boys' hostel, and they lived in the small room at the end of the corridor. At six she asked, "Homework done?" and Rafiq said, "Yes, Ammi," though his maths was still in his bag. Then he went to play carrom in the common room with Kamal. But every time the striker hit, he thought of the lie. At dinner in the mess he couldn't finish his rice. At nine, when the bell rang for lights-out, he found his mother checking the dormitory doors. "Ammi, I lied. The maths isn't done." She stopped, keys in hand. "Thank you for telling me yourself. That matters." Then she pointed at their room. "Now go and finish it. I'll sit with you."

qa.a: She was the matron of the boys' hostel.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel during the evening?
qa.a: Guilty; he kept thinking of the lie and couldn't finish his rice.

qa.q: What else could Rafiq have done at six?
qa.a: Told the truth and finished the maths before carrom.

qa.q: How does Ammi respond to the confession?
qa.a: She thanks him for telling her himself, still has him finish the work, and offers to sit with him.

grounding: A boy who lied about homework feels bad all evening, tells his mother before bed, and she values it while still asking him to finish.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: confessing late after first lying [Revision]
passage: I'm Madhuri, Francis's older sister. On Tuesday Mummy asked Francis if his homework was finished, and he said yes, quickly, and went to watch TV. I knew it wasn't; his notebook lay open on the table with half a page empty. All evening he was strange. He laughed too loudly at the TV, then went quiet at dinner and pushed his dal around. At bedtime I heard him knock on Mummy's door. Through the wall I heard, "Mummy, I lied. I didn't finish." There was a pause. Then Mummy said, "I'm glad you told me. That was brave. Now go and finish it; I'll wait up." He sat at the table till half past ten. He looked tired but, somehow, less heavy.

qa.q: What did Francis do after saying yes?
What might Francis have felt during the evening?
qa.a: Guilty and uneasy, laughing too loudly and then going quiet at dinner.

qa.q: What else could Francis have done when Mummy first asked?
qa.a: Said the homework wasn't done and finished it before TV.

qa.q: How does Madhuri see Francis after he confesses?
qa.a: Madhuri sees him tired but somehow less heavy.

grounding: A sister watches a boy who lied about homework grow uneasy and confess before bed, and their mother respond warmly but firmly.
